content.title: About
content.content: Herring (Clupea harengus) is a marine fish from the Clupeidae family, found in the North Atlantic and Baltic seas. It has a silvery body, a distinctive smell, and firm flesh that is commonly used for pickling, smoking, and in salads.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Herring is one of the most popular fish in Russia and the Nordic countries.
In the 19th century Sweden introduced a "Herring Day" when pickled herring was traditionally served.
Herring can migrate over 2,000 km in search of feeding grounds.
In the Baltic Sea herring plays a key role in the food chain, serving as a main prey for seabirds and marine mammals.
Herring is a staple in traditional dishes such as "herring under a fur coat" and pickled herring.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Herring provides EPA and DHA, polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart and brain health.

items.title: High in vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D from herring aids calcium absorption and supports the immune system.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Protein‑dense
items.content: Herring supplies a complete set of amino acids useful for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Minerals: selenium and iodine
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant, while iodine supports thyroid function.

items.title: Heavy metal content
items.content: Like many marine fish, herring can accumulate mercury; moderate consumption is advised, especially for pregnant women and children.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Salt in pickled herring
items.content: Pickled herring often contains high amounts of salt, which may be unsuitable for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Herring can be eaten fresh, smoked, pickled, or canned. It is added to salads, sandwiches, spreads, and traditional dishes such as "herring under a fur coat".

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh herring fillets should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C for up to 2 days. Smoked and pickled herring store in a sealed container in the fridge for up to a week, while canned herring can be kept in a cool, dry place until the expiration date.
